skill.name: An opening that hooks
skill.why: Readers decide in one line whether to keep reading. Grab them fast.
skill.how: Start with action, a strange detail, a question or someone talking. Skip the weather report.

steps.say: A game that opens on a loading screen? I quit. Readers quit boring first lines too.

show.nudge: Nothing has happened yet. Would you need the next line?

show.text: This is a story about my bin.
show.nudge: It tells you what the story is about. It doesn't make you wonder anything.

steps.ask: Tap the first line that makes you want to read on.
steps.win: Yes! A growling bin? You need to know why. A first line that makes you read on is a hook.

steps.say: Here is how I test a first line. I read it, then ask: do I need the next line?
steps.ask: Why does this line make you read on?

options.reason: Short isn't enough. 'It was a nice day' is short too. What is the bin doing?

options.text: It makes you ask a question: why is it growling?
It tells you what the weather is like.
options.reason: There is no weather in it. Look at what the bin is doing.

steps.win: Right. A hook makes the reader ask a question. Only the next lines can answer it.

steps.say: There are a few ways to hook a reader. Here are three. One has someone talking.

show.text: I was halfway up the flagpole.
show.nudge: Something is happening! But is anyone saying anything?
That is very strange! But look for speech marks. Is anyone talking?

steps.ask: Tap the hook where someone is talking.
steps.win: Yes! Nan's warning makes you need to see inside. Look at the labels: three ways to hook.

steps.say: Questions can hook too. But 'Have you ever…?' is so common that readers skip it.

show.text: Have you ever had a bad day?
show.nudge: That's the one readers skip. It asks about you, not the story.
You can answer yes or no, then stop reading. It's about you, not the story.

show.text: Why was there a goat in the school library?

steps.ask: Tap the question that only the story can answer.
steps.win: Yes! You can't answer it yourself, so you read on. That's a story question.

steps.say: My first draft started like this. It is the other kind of start that readers skip.

show.text: It was a sunny day and I woke up and had toast.

steps.ask: Which line should take its place?

options.text: It was a very, very sunny day.
options.reason: Still the weather. Has anything happened yet?

options.text: I woke up at seven and had toast with jam.
options.reason: Every day starts with waking up. Start where the trouble starts.

options.text: The seagull was back, and this time it had brought friends.

steps.win: Yes! A seagull with friends means trouble is coming. Skip the weather and waking up. Start with the trouble.

steps.say: Use the test on any first line, even your own. Do I need the next line?

show.text: Hi, my name is Mo and I like cooking.

steps.ask: Does Mo's first line hook you?

check.nudge: Use the test. Has anything happened yet? Do you need the next line?

steps.win: Right. It's just facts about Mo. Now test your own first line the same way.

terms.means: A first line that makes the reader ask a question and read on.
Start in the middle of something happening.
Start with something so odd that it needs explaining.
Start with a character's words, like a warning or a secret.
A question only the story can answer. Not 'Have you ever…?'

examples.text: I was halfway up the flagpole

card.test: Read your first line. Do you need the next one? If not, start where the trouble starts.

weDo.frame: Zed is testing three first lines for Gus's lab diary.
weDo.hint: Which one makes you ask a question you need answered?
weDo.success: An empty jar that burps is strange. You have to read on to find out why.

options.text: The jar on Gus's bench was empty. Then it burped.
One morning Gus woke up and went into his lab.
options.reason: This just starts the day. Nothing has happened yet, so there's no reason to keep reading.

options.text: This is a story about Gus and his slime experiment.
options.reason: It tells us what the story is about instead of pulling us into it.

weDo.frame: The crew wrote first lines for the ship's story night.
weDo.prompt: Put each first line in the right bin.
weDo.hint: Does something happen, or is it just setting things up?
weDo.success: Hooks start with action, a puzzle, a question or talk. Plain facts and weather can wait.

items.text: Mo's pie exploded at 6:14 on a Tuesday.
items.reason: An exploding pie drops you straight into the action.

items.text: My name is Tully and I am eleven years old.
items.reason: It's just facts about the writer. Nothing is happening yet.

items.text: Why was the footy covered in green slime?
items.reason: It's a question you want answered, so you keep reading.

items.text: It was a sunny day at the beach.
items.reason: It tells us the weather, but nothing strange or exciting has happened.
Someone is talking, and it's a warning. Now you need to know what's in the box.

creature.name: Dangleby
creature.blurb: A glow-worm that dangles shining threads over the bay. Whatever touches the first glowing bead is hooked for good.

workshop.mentor: The bin was growling. Not a little rumble, either. A proper, deep-in-the-belly growl, like a dog that's spotted the postie. I stood at the end of the driveway in my pyjamas, holding a bag of last night's fish heads, and wondered if I should just go back to bed. Then the lid lifted. Two green eyes blinked at me from the dark. 'Took you long enough,' said the bin.
workshop.ask: Write an opening that hooks. Ideas: a bin that talks, Maxx's cage left open, a footy that won't stop bouncing, a smell under your bed.
checklist: I started with action, a strange detail or a question.
I left my reader wanting to know more.
I skipped the weather and the alarm clock.
I read my first line aloud to test it.
